# Chicago Lease Entry Notice Checklist

A landlord entering without the required 24 hours’ notice can be documented clearly and addressed without escalating too fast. The goal is to preserve evidence, set a paper trail, and ask for a remedy in a calm, firm way.

## Practical Steps After the Entry

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/clipboard-check.svg

- Save the text message, including the sender, date, and time.
- Write a short incident log: date of entry, approximate time, when you learned about it, and what the landlord said it was for.
- Save your lease clause about notice and any addenda about entry, repairs, or emergencies.
- If you have them, keep photos, video, smart-lock logs, doorbell logs, building access logs, or witness notes.
- Note whether there was any actual emergency, visible damage, or later proof that the visit was truly urgent.
- Keep all communication in writing from this point forward.
- If the landlord enters again, document it immediately the same way.

## Polite but Firm Message to Send

Media: Icon=https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap-icons@1.11.3/icons/chat-left-text.svg

Hello [Landlord Name],

I’m writing about the entry into my apartment on 2026-02-18. My lease requires 24 hours’ notice for non-emergency entry, and I did not receive prior notice before this visit.

I understand you said afterward that it was for a water leak inspection. Please confirm:
- the reason for the entry,
- whether there was an actual emergency,
- who entered the unit,
- and whether you will make sure future non-emergency entries follow the lease notice requirement.

Please also keep all future entry requests in writing and provide advance notice unless there is a true emergency.

Thank you,
[Your Name]
[Unit Number]

## Remedies Tenants Commonly Request


- Written acknowledgment that the entry did not follow the lease notice rule.
- A commitment to give proper advance notice for all future non-emergency entries.
- A management policy reminder or internal correction so it does not happen again.
- Repair of any damage, if the entry caused damage or disturbed belongings.
- Rent credit or fee waiver in some cases, especially if the entry was repeated or disruptive.
- A right to be present for future inspections or maintenance visits when practical.
- A move to formal complaint channels if the issue continues.

## What Usually Helps Your Position

- Keep the tone factual, not emotional.
- Use the lease language exactly as written.
- Separate the notice problem from any actual maintenance issue.
- If the landlord claims an emergency, ask for the specific facts supporting that claim.
- If there were repeated entries, document each one separately.
